# Abstract {.unnumbered}

This Element asks a basic question: why do some policy actors change their minds when new information arrives, while others do not? We develop a model of policy learning that focuses on how people weigh new information against what they already believe, explaining why some information shifts beliefs while other information gets ignored or reinterpreted to fit prior views. We test the model using nearly two decades of survey data on US public opinion about nuclear energy, tracing how beliefs and support for building new nuclear power plants changed after the 2011 Fukushima accident. We then place this model of individual learning within the broader policymaking process, showing how the same information can lead to different learning outcomes, or none at all, depending on the coalitions, institutions, and political context involved; we illustrate this with brief comparisons of how Germany, Japan, Italy, China, the United Kingdom, France, and the United States responded to Fukushima. Finally, we connect the model back to the wider policy learning literature, showing how it helps address a long-standing puzzle in the field: why learning among individuals does not always add up to learning, or policy change, across an entire political system. We close by discussing the limits of this approach and directions for future research.

**Keywords**: Policy learning; Information processing; Belief change; Nuclear energy; Public opinion
